blocks.text: Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at Florida’s property tax rollback, projected PCB shortages, the end of Tesla’s Cybertruck, the lack of progress in carbon storage, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

Housekeeping items this week: I accidentally emailed out this week’s essay, How Do Building Codes Affect the Price of Housing, to paid members only instead of all subscribers. This has been fixed, and it’s available now for everyone. I think a couple people may have signed up for paid subscriptions specifically because of this — if this is you, let me know and I’ll issue you a refund.

From the annals of “the return of the property tax revolt”: this week Florida approved an amendment to exempt a larger portion of a person’s home from property tax. It’s estimated to reduce government revenues by nearly $5 billion in 2027-2028 alone. [HousingWire]

And from the annals of “frontier AI models are surprisingly capable at things you wouldn’t expect them to be”: AI models are apparently now pretty good at generating permit-quality construction documents. People have been making flavors of this claim for a while, but this is the first time I’ve seen it made from an actual architect. “Drawing upon my background as an architect, I tested 13 older and newly released AI models to measure their technical drawing abilities. I found that the strongest drafting model at the time of writing is Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, released in September of 2026. With some skilled guidance, Opus 5.5 is capable of producing sophisticated drafting and permit-quality architectural drawing sets for simple buildings.” [Substack]

A new paper estimates that wildfire risk to US buildings could triple by 2060. “We reconstruct fire risk to structures from 1945-2023 and project its evolution through 2060 across the U.S. using high-resolution historical data on area burned, settlement patterns, and fire impacts. Under business-as-usual conditions with no adaptation, structural losses are projected to nearly triple nationwide, with 133,200–449,100 buildings expected to be damaged or destroyed by mid-century.” [Nature]

Opponents of a housing project being planned above a San Francisco Safeway are suing the project under a provision of the 1871 Civil Rights Act, originally passed to combat violence from the Ku Klux Klan. [HousingWire]

Chinese robot manufacturer Unitree’s factory operations remain (surprisingly?) manual. “At the end of 2025 all of Unitree’s machinery was worth about $1.7 million on its books, at a company that made almost 32,000 robots that year: some $50 of machinery per robot!” [X]
One of Intel’s fabs in Israel was shut down for 2 weeks after an explosion that killed two people, possibly due to a gas cylinder malfunction. [Tom’s Hardware]

Are printed circuit boards the next AI datacenter-induced component shortage? “We’ve seen huge demand/supply driven price rises in RAM, GPUs, SSDs, and more through 2026. Now that most basic and unglamorous electronics necessity, the PCB, looks set to join them. A news report published by Nikkei Asia quotes several leading PC and PCB industry managers, making it clear we are going to see PCB (and PCB subcomponent) shortages and price rises in the coming months.” [Tom’s Hardware]
BYD sold more electric vehicles in October than the entire US did the entire third quarter. [Electrek] And more than 50% of heavy trucks sold in China in September were EVs. [Electrek]

Blake Scholl, CEO of supersonic airliner startup Boom, says it’s now spending most of its resources working on the power-generating gas turbine for AI data centers, and once that’s been developed it will shift focus back to the airliner. [X] Related, if any of my readers work at Kalshi or Polymarket, I would love a prediction market for the Boom airliner.
Related, I liked this idea from Scholl: use AI to check for weird edge cases in aircraft flight control software. [X]

JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine's "Against Tech Oligarchy" (permalink)

JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine are veterans of a string of hard-fought unionization drives at tech workplaces that started with some astounding successes but ran up against ferocious resistance in the second Trump term; their book about tech labor, Against Tech Oligarchy, is a superb analysis of the challenges and potential for tech labor organizing:
https://againsttecholigarchy.com/

For decades, tech workers enjoyed extraordinary power, despite the fact that virtually no tech workers were in unions. That's because tech workers were both extremely valuable to their employers (each engineer hired by a Silicon Valley firm added about $1m to the company's bottom line) and extremely scarce.

This won tech workers very favorable working conditions, high compensation, and a great deal of control over their employers' products (because if a worker refused to work on a project, it was hard to find someone else to do the work). What's more, there has always been a sizable cohort of tech workers whose own lives were profoundly improved by access to digital networks and wanted more than anything to distribute those benefits to everyone else. I call these workers "Tron-pilled," because they fought for the user:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/11/obvious-terrible-ideas/#bayesian-terrorism

During the era of tech worker scarcity, few tech workers saw themselves as workers at all – rather, the tech worker's self-conception was as an entrepreneur in waiting, a temporarily embarrassed founder. Tech bosses played on this perception, promoting the idea of tech workers and managers as peers and/or family members. Tech CEOs affected hoodies and jeans and hosted company-wide meetings where they allowed engineers to pepper them with impertinent questions about the company's technical and commercial direction.

But scarcity-based power only lasts until supply catches up with demand. As the number of workers outstripped the number of jobs, bosses showed their true colors. That's what happened at Kickstarter, when one of the bosses forced out his co-founders and declared himself CEO and proceeded to override the decisions of the company's Trust and Safety team. This sparked one of tech's first unionization drives, and it was a bitter fight, with management pulling out every dirty tactic in the union-busting playbook:
https://kickstarterunited.org/oral-history/

The labor militancy at Kickstarter United wasn't an isolated incident. Workers at much bigger companies like Google and Microsoft had a long tradition of pushing back against management through internal channels, open letters, and, starting in 2018, mass walkouts:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Google_walkouts

But post-Trump, bosses at these companies were much less willing to countenance dissent, and waves of vicious retaliation and reprisals radicalized many workers at these companies, driving them to more traditional, organized forms of labor activism. At the same time, workers at smaller, "mission-driven" shops like Bandcamp were inspired by the success of Kickstarter United and they started their own drives. All this attracted the interest of the "internationals" – big, established unions like the Communications Workers of America – who trained union organizers at all kinds of tech shops and started laying the groundwork for traditional union drives.

Most of Against Tech Oligarchy tells the story of these drives in a gripping you-are-there style (it helps that both of the authors are veterans of several of these campaigns). The stakes get much higher during the pandemic, of course, as tech comes to play a more central role in the lives of hundreds of millions of locked-down workers, and as the tech companies themselves went on uncontrolled hiring sprees, putting workers on the payroll without any duties or responsibilities, often just to ensure that a rival company couldn't hire them.

The pandemic also prompted many tech bosses to express far more worker-hostile sentiments than they'd ever let slip in public before. Fully remote workforces both frustrated tech bosses and also significantly reduced the opportunities for in-person labor organizing. All of this built to a series of rising crescendos, such as Musk's Twitter takeover and mass layoffs, and Israel's tech-fueled genocide in Gaza. Confrontations between tech workers and bosses grew more bitter and direct, even as solidarity between white-collar tech workers and their blue-collar peers (notably Amazon warehouse workers) increased.

If all Against Tech Oligarchy did was lay out the cut-and-thrust of these labor struggles during these momentous years, it would be worth the price of admission. But it's in the final chapters that the book really distinguishes itself, because it's here that the authors embark on a pitiless postmortem of their own failed campaigns and the failures of their peers and ask themselves what it will take to unionize tech workers.

They start with the observation that most American union organizing is built around maintaining "labor peace" (by swiftly moving to recognition and a contract) but that tech bosses are ready to wage "labor war" (through illegal union-busting and retaliation). A labor peace strategy avoids costly and dangerous risks to established unions, such as decertification of locals and expensive and bruising court battles. But for tech bosses, labor war pays off, because their workforce is transient, fragmented, and skeptical of the very idea that they are workers. They have little to no experience with unions and can barely imagine how a union might improve their working lives.

The traditional labor playbook calls for workers to quietly build their power, taking no overt action while conducting a series of personal, one-to-one conversations that contribute to an eventual quorum of workers that's large enough to win a unionization vote. This strategy is like building a bonfire, where the pieces of fuel are piled one atop the other, but not lit until the pile is done.

But in a tech shop where workers turn over frequently and work in isolated teams, often from home, this strategy fails. Workers who have been won to the union side leave or grow demoralized in their isolation. Reaching new workers is difficult, and since the whole union drive occurs in secret, new workers don't know to reach out to organizers in their shops.

For Tan and Redwine, this fact militates for a strategy that revives some of the pre-labor activism of tech workers, noisy public/private fights whenever product decisions and management conduct violates some mix of worker rights and workers' values. They see this as a way to build momentum within a shop, bringing workers off the sidelines and giving organizers chances to bring those workers into a sustained, structured labor drive.

Tan and Redwine see tech worker organizing as the frontrunners of an age of new labor militancy and labor war, of the sort that pre-dated the labor peace that arose after the passage of the National Labor Relations Act. That labor peace was the result of bosses learning that hardball tactics would be met with equally hardcore responses.

This is especially important for tech workers, whose strikes cannot inflict the same pain on their bosses as earlier industrial workers' strikes did. Digital systems are designed to operate themselves after their are built, so when the workers involved in those systems withdraw their labor, the systems continue to run, often for a very long time, before needing maintenance (this is also the lesson of Musk's mass layoffs at Twitter).

Tech bosses have metabolized this lesson, and they are increasingly willing to wage all-out war at the first sign of labor unrest, with waves of retaliatory firings. These bosses have figured out devilish tactics for constructive dismissal, like the CEO of Mapbox, who retaliated against union supporters by targeting them with "return to office" mandates that forced them to report in person to offices that were in distant states. This prompted many of these workers to quit, which spared Mapbox from even paying them a severance package.

Against this backdrop, strikes need to be seen not as a way to bring the business operations to a halt, but rather as a way to galvanize workers and bring them into the union drive. As New York Times Tech Guild organizer John Cruickshank put it, Action builds capacity for action.

This is the ethos of the Microsoft workers who have campaigned tirelessly to halt the company's participation in the genocide in Gaza. They barricaded themselves in executives' offices, livestreaming the confrontation; they disrupted Microsoft's livecast 50th anniversary celebration; and they paddled a flotilla of protest kayaks outside of top Microsoft executives' waterfront homes. All of this paid off, with Microsoft halting sales of its tools to a particularly notorious unit of the Israeli military who had been using the company's products to conduct surveillance in Gaza and the West Bank.

Tan and Redwine see these novel tactics as a rewilding of the labor movement, a return to the militant roots that led to the labor peace, but only after all-out labor war. They cite the 1934 Minneapolis truck drivers' strike, where workers invented the "flying picket" by swarming scab trucks far from the factory gates, defeating the trucks' police protection, which led to a general strike and a total victory for labor.

This is important historical context. The genteel business of getting everyone's cards signed and having the NLRB certify your union was the compromise bosses agreed to after they learned that the alternative was far worse for them. Today, it's not just bosses who've forgotten that lesson – many workers have, too. Against Tech Oligarchy aims to rekindle those old boilers and get the unstoppable labor train running again.

The stakes get much higher during the pandemic, of course, as tech comes to play a more central role in the lives of hundreds of millions of locked-down workers, and as the tech companies themselves went on uncontrolled hiring sprees, putting workers on the payroll without any duties or responsibilities, often just to ensure that a rival company couldn't hire them.

The pandemic also prompted many tech bosses to express far more worker-hostile sentiments than they'd ever let slip in public before. Fully remote workforces both frustrated tech bosses and also significantly reduced the opportunities for in-person labor organizing. All of this built to a series of rising crescendos, such as Musk's Twitter takeover and mass layoffs, and Israel's tech-fueled genocide in Gaza. Confrontations between tech workers and bosses grew more bitter and direct, even as solidarity between white-collar tech workers and their blue-collar peers (notably Amazon warehouse workers) increased.

If all Against Tech Oligarchy did was lay out the cut-and-thrust of these labor struggles during these momentous years, it would be worth the price of admission. But it's in the final chapters that the book really distinguishes itself, because it's here that the authors embark on a pitiless postmortem of their own failed campaigns and the failures of their peers and ask themselves what it will take to unionize tech workers.

They start with the observation that most American union organizing is built around maintaining "labor peace" (by swiftly moving to recognition and a contract) but that tech bosses are ready to wage "labor war" (through illegal union-busting and retaliation). A labor peace strategy avoids costly and dangerous risks to established unions, such as decertification of locals and expensive and bruising court battles. But for tech bosses, labor war pays off, because their workforce is transient, fragmented, and skeptical of the very idea that they are workers. They have little to no experience with unions and can barely imagine how a union might improve their working lives.

The traditional labor playbook calls for workers to quietly build their power, taking no overt action while conducting a series of personal, one-to-one conversations that contribute to an eventual quorum of workers that's large enough to win a unionization vote. This strategy is like building a bonfire, where the pieces of fuel are piled one atop the other, but not lit until the pile is done.

But in a tech shop where workers turn over frequently and work in isolated teams, often from home, this strategy fails. Workers who have been won to the union side leave or grow demoralized in their isolation. Reaching new workers is difficult, and since the whole union drive occurs in secret, new workers don't know to reach out to organizers in their shops.

For Tan and Redwine, this fact militates for a strategy that revives some of the pre-labor activism of tech workers, noisy public/private fights whenever product decisions and management conduct violates some mix of worker rights and workers' values. They see this as a way to build momentum within a shop, bringing workers off the sidelines and giving organizers chances to bring those workers into a sustained, structured labor drive.

Tan and Redwine see tech worker organizing as the frontrunners of an age of new labor militancy and labor war, of the sort that pre-dated the labor peace that arose after the passage of the National Labor Relations Act. That labor peace was the result of bosses learning that hardball tactics would be met with equally hardcore responses.

This is especially important for tech workers, whose strikes cannot inflict the same pain on their bosses as earlier industrial workers' strikes did. Digital systems are designed to operate themselves after their are built, so when the workers involved in those systems withdraw their labor, the systems continue to run, often for a very long time, before needing maintenance (this is also the lesson of Musk's mass layoffs at Twitter).

Tech bosses have metabolized this lesson, and they are increasingly willing to wage all-out war at the first sign of labor unrest, with waves of retaliatory firings. These bosses have figured out devilish tactics for constructive dismissal, like the CEO of Mapbox, who retaliated against union supporters by targeting them with "return to office" mandates that forced them to report in person to offices that were in distant states. This prompted many of these workers to quit, which spared Mapbox from even paying them a severance package.

Against this backdrop, strikes need to be seen not as a way to bring the business operations to a halt, but rather as a way to galvanize workers and bring them into the union drive. As New York Times Tech Guild organizer John Cruickshank put it, Action builds capacity for action.

This is the ethos of the Microsoft workers who have campaigned tirelessly to halt the company's participation in the genocide in Gaza. They barricaded themselves in executives' offices, livestreaming the confrontation; they disrupted Microsoft's livecast 50th anniversary celebration; and they paddled a flotilla of protest kayaks outside of top Microsoft executives' waterfront homes. All of this paid off, with Microsoft halting sales of its tools to a particularly notorious unit of the Israeli military who had been using the company's products to conduct surveillance in Gaza and the West Bank.

Tan and Redwine see these novel tactics as a rewilding of the labor movement, a return to the militant roots that led to the labor peace, but only after all-out labor war. They cite the 1934 Minneapolis truck drivers' strike, where workers invented the "flying picket" by swarming scab trucks far from the factory gates, defeating the trucks' police protection, which led to a general strike and a total victory for labor.

This is important historical context. The genteel business of getting everyone's cards signed and having the NLRB certify your union was the compromise bosses agreed to after they learned that the alternative was far worse for them. Today, it's not just bosses who've forgotten that lesson – many workers have, too. Against Tech Oligarchy aims to rekindle those old boilers and get the unstoppable labor train running again.

blocks.text: This is a difficult but essential book. I was initially put off by how graphically autobiographical it is. The disaster planning I came for was frequently interrupted with the author's loves, disasters, health issues, pains, and domestic issues. As the book wore on, I realised how vital that is. Disasters - whether natural or caused by human actions - cannot be tackled in a dispassionate way. It's all very well having a plan to repatriate bodies, strict timetables for witness statements, and a clinical approach to disposing of victims' personal effects - but there needs to be space for a humane response; not just a humanitarian response. People need space to grieve, they need a shower and cup of tea, they need to be allowed to fucking scream.
My chauvinistic biases were stopped in their tracks by the unrelenting assault of pure and righteous indignation.
Women in disaster planning and response are constantly accused of overreaction, of too much thinking and emotion. We ignore our instincts in an effort to fit in.

It is also a rallying cry against the national crime that was austerity. The hollowing out of the state's capacity to respond to trauma was a vicious and unnecessary attack on our future. Hoping that the worst never comes is in itself a recipe for disaster.
The book is necessarily grim - with occasional gallows humour - but never fails to be fascinating:
It seemed that pigeons and other birds were scooping up the smallest human bones, the finger bones or phalanges, that were still being uncovered

Every chapter contains at least one "big ooof" where you can see exactly how reality refuses to comply to with the best laid plans of disaster planners. Here's one about the difficulty in identifying people after a disaster:
[The victims] had the same kit on and, in an extra twist of fate, they had all dyed their hair canary yellow for the game.
As I said, it is a difficult and bloody book. Vital reading for anyone who wants to understand the why and the how of complex recovery efforts.

blocks.text: The Marx diesel freight train set number 9613 was an early 1950s electric train set featuring twin diesel locomotives pulling 7-inch freight cars, sold through Montgomery Ward. It’s an attractive set and a very good example of post-war tin lithography, which was becoming something of a lost art at the time.
Marx diesel type electrical train set 9613

The set consisted of two diesel locomotives numbered 6000, one powered and one dummy unit, and a caboose lettered for the Southern Pacific, which was one of the largest railroads west of the Mississippi River at the time. The diesels and caboose flanked the following 7-inch cars to make a five-unit set:
Pennsylvania Merchandise Service boxcar, any number from 37950-37959
Wabash gondola, yellow, number 80982

The powered engine had both forward and reverse, so the 9613 set could compete very nicely with a Lionel Scout set. The price and capabilities were similar, but Lionel didn’t offer diesel locomotives at that price point. So the Marx set looked less dated than what Lionel was willing to sell at a similar price.
This set is very similar to set 9500, but this version was for Montgomery Ward.
Other set contents

The 9613 set also included an oval of O27 track and a 50 watt transformer, model 1249 with circuit breaker. This transformer had a set of fixed-voltage posts for accessories running at 13 volts. Marx often gave exclusives to big retailers that were very similar to sets everyone else sold. Marx set 9613’s special thing that made it exclusive was including a slightly nicer transformer. The wattage was the same, but the transformer in the 9500 set didn’t have the accessory posts.

Having the nicer transformer gave Montgomery Ward a chance to push powered accessories as an add-on with the set. Or to sell accessories to them the next year. Part of the business model was to sell the train set one year, and sell expansions for several years after.
What was Southern Pacific?

The Southern Pacific was a Class 1 railroad that operated mostly in the southwestern United States, operating around 13,000 miles of track at its peak. Its track ran through the major cities in California, so this set would have had more appeal in the western United States than a set lettered for, say, the New York Central or Pennsylvania railroads.

The Southern Pacific merged into the Union Pacific in 1996. Southern Pacific has an interesting history beyond railroads. It ran telegraph lines alongside its railroad tracks, taking advantage of the value of the right-of-way, and in the 1970s it started using those lines for long distance telephone calls in competition with AT&T. They called the service Sprint and eventually spun it off into a separate business, the telephone company that merged with T-Mobile in 2020.
Other sets lettered for the Southern Pacific include the aforementioned 9500 set and the 9365 steam set.
Value

I typically see boxed examples of the 9613 set sell for around $100 shipped. Having original paperwork and a box in nice condition helps the value. Boxed examples are reasonably common, because Marx shipped them in sturdy boxes that worked well for storage, and the owners frequently boxed the set back up for storage when they weren’t using it.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

blocks.text: It seems like Dell Optiplex computers get a lot of attention, but I’ve had better luck recently finding HP Elitedesk PCs. These compete with the Dell Optiplex, and they have a lot of the same advantages and disadvantages. In this blog post, I will walk through upgrades I used to turn a used HP Elitedesk 800 G4 into a viable gaming and streaming PC running Windows 11.
Curing the small form factor blues

First off, I got the small form factor version. Don’t judge me. Of course I would have bought the mini tower if I could have found one. At the time of purchase, the only mid tower computer I could find with a new enough CPU to run for Windows 11 would have required me to drive halfway to Chicago.
That’s not altogether a bad thing. I figure a lot of people will have questions about how to upgrade the small form factor versions of these machines.
SSD upgrade options for an HP Elitedesk 800 G4

To work on them, there is a latch on the back that you slide that releases the top cover. Then the top cover slides forward. The motherboard has a position for an NVMe SSD, and there are also a pair of 3.5-inch drive bays that can accept either a conventional hard drive or SSD. Any SSD is a huge upgrade over a conventional hard drive, but if the system doesn’t have an NVMe drive, I recommend installing one of those. They are faster than a SATA SSD, all other things being equal. Price on NVMe drives has also come down. You used to pay a premium for them just because they were faster. Not so much anymore.

There are more SATA ports on the motherboard than there are drive bays, but you can take advantage of them by buying a 2.5 to 3.5 adapter that has room for two SSDs. The dual drive adapters usually don’t cost any more than a single drive adapter does, and that will give you enough room inside for a total of four drives, plus the NVMe drive. We didn’t have an immediate need to install any additional storage, but we have plenty of options when that time comes.
Maximum RAM upgrade for HP Elitedesk 800 G4

The HP Elitedesk 800 G4 uses DDR4 RAM. Mine had a single 8 MB module installed in one of its four slots. I had a matched pair of four gigabyte modules and another matched pair of 8 GB modules, so I installed those for a total of 24 GB. The system can take up to 64 GB, in the form of (4) 16 GB modules. I will eventually do that, but memory prices being where they are, 24 will have to do for a while.
For best performance, install matched pairs of modules in the color coded sockets. One pair of sockets is black and the other pair is white.
Video card upgrade for HP Elitedesk 800 G4
The Intel integrated graphics are perfectly fine for running office applications, but they are not fine for streaming. OBS doesn’t like them.

We found a low profile RTX 3050. It cost considerably more than the rest of the computer, but that generation of Nvidia video cards can do some interesting things, and I imagine it’s an upgrade a lot of people who buy a system like this will be interested in. For our purposes, it is able to do hardware based encoding in OBS, and that isn’t the case with, say, a GT 1030.

Make sure you buy the low profile version, ideally, the one from MSI. MSI’s low profile version will fit and it does not need the supplemental PCI Express power connector. That’s a good thing, because this machine doesn’t have one of those.

I had to swap the bracket with the low profile version, but that wasn’t a huge deal. The card came bundled with the low profile bracket. If you buy one used, it’s definitely worth asking whether it comes with both brackets. Whichever bracket you don’t end up using easily gets lost.

I’d almost buy the low profile version of the 3050 even for a full-size PC, because it doesn’t require the PCI Express connector, and it fits in either a small form factor system or systems with the more conventional form factor. If you decide to upgrade from it, the low profile version will likely have more demand. Especially the MSI version that fits in more machines without modification.
I had to modify the case to make the Gigabyte RTX 3050 fit. But we couldn’t get an MSI, so we made the Gigabyte work.
Conclusion

The HP Elitedesk 800 G4 is a reasonably well built PC with a lot to offer. The case is flimsier than older HP models, but the motherboard and chipset are great, and business class PCs tend to run Windows really well as long as you give them enough memory, a fast SSD, and a fast video card. The corporate security tools that bog down your work PC aren’t a factor when you use the same hardware to build a PC for home use.

Corporations are discarding these systems because they are now out of warranty, but they are fully supported for Windows 11, and when you run a clean install from the Microsoft ISO, an upgraded Elitedesk runs Windows 11 rather well. I have some tips for moving your user profile to the new PC if you need them. If you want to use a local account, which Microsoft makes unnecessarily difficult, I have tips for that too.
I have several older Windows 10 PCs I keep around for experimentation purposes and as spares. I will definitely be looking for more Elitedesk 800 G4 or similar systems to replace them with.

translations: It seems like Dell Optiplex computers get a lot of attention, but I’ve had better luck recently finding HP Elitedesk PCs. These compete with the Dell Optiplex, and they have a lot of the same advantages and disadvantages. In this blog post, I will walk through upgrades I used to turn a used HP Elitedesk 800 G4 into a viable gaming and streaming PC running Windows 11.
Curing the small form factor blues

First off, I got the small form factor version. Don’t judge me. Of course I would have bought the mini tower if I could have found one. At the time of purchase, the only mid tower computer I could find with a new enough CPU to run for Windows 11 would have required me to drive halfway to Chicago.
That’s not altogether a bad thing. I figure a lot of people will have questions about how to upgrade the small form factor versions of these machines.
SSD upgrade options for an HP Elitedesk 800 G4

To work on them, there is a latch on the back that you slide that releases the top cover. Then the top cover slides forward. The motherboard has a position for an NVMe SSD, and there are also a pair of 3.5-inch drive bays that can accept either a conventional hard drive or SSD. Any SSD is a huge upgrade over a conventional hard drive, but if the system doesn’t have an NVMe drive, I recommend installing one of those. They are faster than a SATA SSD, all other things being equal. Price on NVMe drives has also come down. You used to pay a premium for them just because they were faster. Not so much anymore.

There are more SATA ports on the motherboard than there are drive bays, but you can take advantage of them by buying a 2.5 to 3.5 adapter that has room for two SSDs. The dual drive adapters usually don’t cost any more than a single drive adapter does, and that will give you enough room inside for a total of four drives, plus the NVMe drive. We didn’t have an immediate need to install any additional storage, but we have plenty of options when that time comes.
Maximum RAM upgrade for HP Elitedesk 800 G4

The HP Elitedesk 800 G4 uses DDR4 RAM. Mine had a single 8 MB module installed in one of its four slots. I had a matched pair of four gigabyte modules and another matched pair of 8 GB modules, so I installed those for a total of 24 GB. The system can take up to 64 GB, in the form of (4) 16 GB modules. I will eventually do that, but memory prices being where they are, 24 will have to do for a while.
For best performance, install matched pairs of modules in the color coded sockets. One pair of sockets is black and the other pair is white.
Video card upgrade for HP Elitedesk 800 G4
The Intel integrated graphics are perfectly fine for running office applications, but they are not fine for streaming. OBS doesn’t like them.

We found a low profile RTX 3050. It cost considerably more than the rest of the computer, but that generation of Nvidia video cards can do some interesting things, and I imagine it’s an upgrade a lot of people who buy a system like this will be interested in. For our purposes, it is able to do hardware based encoding in OBS, and that isn’t the case with, say, a GT 1030.

Make sure you buy the low profile version, ideally, the one from MSI. MSI’s low profile version will fit and it does not need the supplemental PCI Express power connector. That’s a good thing, because this machine doesn’t have one of those.

I had to swap the bracket with the low profile version, but that wasn’t a huge deal. The card came bundled with the low profile bracket. If you buy one used, it’s definitely worth asking whether it comes with both brackets. Whichever bracket you don’t end up using easily gets lost.

I’d almost buy the low profile version of the 3050 even for a full-size PC, because it doesn’t require the PCI Express connector, and it fits in either a small form factor system or systems with the more conventional form factor. If you decide to upgrade from it, the low profile version will likely have more demand. Especially the MSI version that fits in more machines without modification.
I had to modify the case to make the Gigabyte RTX 3050 fit. But we couldn’t get an MSI, so we made the Gigabyte work.
Conclusion

The HP Elitedesk 800 G4 is a reasonably well built PC with a lot to offer. The case is flimsier than older HP models, but the motherboard and chipset are great, and business class PCs tend to run Windows really well as long as you give them enough memory, a fast SSD, and a fast video card. The corporate security tools that bog down your work PC aren’t a factor when you use the same hardware to build a PC for home use.

Corporations are discarding these systems because they are now out of warranty, but they are fully supported for Windows 11, and when you run a clean install from the Microsoft ISO, an upgraded Elitedesk runs Windows 11 rather well. I have some tips for moving your user profile to the new PC if you need them. If you want to use a local account, which Microsoft makes unnecessarily difficult, I have tips for that too.

blocks.text: This week’s package management news, gathered from the package manager OPML feed collection, my posts and boosts on Mastodon, and anything people sent me. Version control and forge news is in the Wednesday This Week in Source Control roundup.
Security

Vox Pupuli fixed three critical vulnerabilities that a Neodyme researcher reported in OpenVox, the community fork of Puppet. OpenVox Server deserialised Ruby objects embedded in agent run reports, which allowed remote code execution. The shared Trapperkeeper authorisation library matched every plain-string rule in auth.conf as a wildcard, so a certificate for evil.target.example.com was accepted as target.example.com. The OpenVoxDB container image allowed any certificate to reach its API because its allowlist script failed on startup.

All known Puppet implementations are affected, and the fixes are in openvox-agent 8.32.0 and 9.3.0 and openvox-server and openvoxdb 8.18.0 and 9.2.0. Updates to open source Puppet, including security fixes, have ended, so Vox Pupuli recommends migrating to OpenVox.

An issue on actions/runner-images reports that GitHub’s public macOS runners still accept certificates from the compromised eMudhra intermediates covered here last week. Apple has yet to patch the system /etc/ssl/cert.pem. Homebrew has shipped patched ca-certificates, curl and git, but the runner images disable Homebrew updates, so jobs run the vulnerable preinstalled versions.

DSA-6607-1 fixes CVE-2026-109518 in APT, found by Max Justicz. When an HTTP redirect gave two package downloads the same URI, APT could merge them. A retried download then let an attacker on the network path, including a malicious mirror or proxy, replace a package after verification and run code as root.
The attack needs Acquire::Retries set to 1 or higher, and the default is 3 from Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04. Fixed versions are 3.0.4 for trixie, 2.6.2 for bookworm and 3.3.6 in unstable.

A Nixpkgs advisory covers two bugs in darwin.linux-builder, the Linux VM that macOS users run as a remote builder. The run-builder script added the whole keys directory to the world-readable Nix store, so any local user could log in as builder, a trusted user on the VM’s Nix daemon (GHSA-45qr-47fw-2p57).

The QEMU variants also forwarded the builder’s SSH port on every network interface (GHSA-w5j5-2jpq-3cv3). Fixes are on unstable and 26.05, and after updating the advisory says to delete the old key pair from the store, regenerate it and delete the builder’s disk image.
Docker Engine 29.9.3 fixes four CVEs in the engine and SwarmKit. It also updates to BuildKit 0.34.2, which fixes a resolver cache poisoning crash when a build resolves the same Git source twice.
Releases

hex.pm opened Workload Identity and staged publishing to every package and organisation. A GitHub Actions job can exchange its OIDC token for a Workload Identity token that expires after 15 minutes and can publish only that package. An organisation can also use a read identity to fetch its private packages in CI with only the job’s OIDC token. Staged publishing holds releases published with a key or a workload identity until a person approves them with a fresh 2FA code.

New packages get staging by default and existing packages have to opt in. Staged releases expire after seven days. Hex 2.7.0 adds mix hex.publish --wait, which blocks until the release is approved and exits with an error if it is rejected or expires. A new --check-unused-ignores flag makes mix hex.audit fail on ignore entries that match nothing in mix.lock.

PyPI’s redesigned project pages add a Security tab that shows each release’s provenance and the attestations for each file. A release counts as having full provenance only when every file has a Trusted Publisher or SLSA build attestation. Warnings flag incomplete, inconsistent, changed or lost provenance, and files uploaded more than 14 days after an older release get a late-upload marker.

conda 26.10.0 makes conda-rattler-solver the default solver, including after upgrades where the solver setting is unset. --solver=libmamba selects the libmamba solver, and the classic pycosat solver now ships in a bundled conda-pycosat-solver plugin. The release also records when an environment was last activated and adds --disable-plugins and --enable-plugins for switching individual plugins off and on.

pnpm 12.18.0 publishes platform variants of a package to pnpr registries as one archive per target, and installs the variant that fits the host. Publishing to any other registry requires --no-variants, which publishes only the archive that targets any platform. Agent skills are now approved one skill at a time and linked under their own names. pnpr 0.1.0-alpha.18 stores hosted package metadata in SQLite or libSQL and logs release records in transparency logs.

mise 2026.11.0 (now 2026.11.3) makes --locked require checksums, and safe mode now ignores project lockfiles. It adds opt-in Sigstore provenance verification for npm: tools, which checks only the tool’s own package and requires the embedded aube package manager. Tasks can now declare a lock so that runs sharing a database or simulator execute one at a time, even across worktrees.

pixi 0.84.0 (now 0.84.1) moves exclude-newer into the [workspace] table and supports exemptions to the cutoff. A workspace can apply the cutoff to new releases by default and exempt vetted security releases. A rattler fix for hash collisions between unequal package versions means lockfiles written by older pixi versions may require a pixi lock before pixi accepts them as locked.

pip 26.3 blocks unexpected imports during installation and warns about unsafe ones afterwards. HTTP redirects to file: URLs are now rejected, and PyPI’s restriction on direct URL dependencies now covers extras and cached wheels. -r pylock.toml now supports extras and non-default dependency groups, and accepts --no-binary. The security policy now states that installing untrusted wheels has always been unsafe, since Python’s import system can run third-party code during installation.

Gradle 9.9.0 promotes the custom dependencies block API out of incubation, including bundles and constraints from providers. When the wrapper task regenerates gradle-wrapper.properties, it now carries over existing settings such as distribution type, timeouts and retries. It still regenerates distributionUrl, which overwrites a custom host.
zizmor 1.32.0 adds experimental support for GitHub’s new workflow lockfiles. It now collects only the inputs GitHub Actions reads, so it skips workflows in vendored directories.

Renovate 44.210.0 to 44.222.0 adds a julia manager with a datasource for the General registry and Julia versioning, and reads transitive dependencies from uv.lock for security updates. Extracted constraints are now shared across managers. A tool version pinned in mise or rust-toolchain limits the updates other managers open.

Dependabot version updates now support Microsoft’s Agent Package Manager on github.com, following the apm ecosystem added in Dependabot Core 0.400.0. It opens pull requests for git dependencies declared in apm.yml and regenerates apm.lock.yaml when present. The support covers version updates only.

Articles

Friction in the Python Packaging Standards Process (konsti, uv) lists problems with how packaging PEPs get made. The text goes through editing passes before and after discussion and moves between reStructuredText and Markdown. Discussions on discuss.python.org have no concern tracking, and several maintainers avoid the forum. Small changes, such as removing a decade-old unimplemented feature, require a full PEP. The post points to Rust’s RFC concern tracking and final comment period as prior art.

Scrutinize our assessments (Daniel Stenberg) follows up on curl moving low and medium severity vulnerability handling into public GitHub issues. Stenberg explains the vuln:ASSESS, vuln:NONE, vuln:LOW and vuln:MEDIUM labels and asks outsiders to challenge the severity calls. CVE IDs are visible from assignment, and the full records are published on the release date.

The author of No, npm, “estee” is not a typo of “testem” (smoores.dev) hit npm’s typosquat check while naming a package for the Storyteller project. The registry rejected estee as too similar to espree and testem, then flagged the fallback hoid against hoek, hono, uuid and zod. npm support declined to lift the automated block. The author infers an edit-distance-of-two rule against popular names. Under that rule preact and estree would also be blocked.

The intensional model in disguise (Farid Zakaria) maps Nix onto Bazel and buck2. Bazel and buck2 key actions by the content of their inputs, so editing a comment in a C file stops the rebuild once the compiled output comes out the same. Nix gets that early cutoff only with content-addressed derivations, because by default it addresses outputs by their recipe. The post lines up Nix’s resolved derivations, realisations and store with Bazel’s actions, action cache and CAS.

Josh Bressers talked to Roi Nisimi about backport gaps: security fixes merged to a project’s main branch but missing from its latest release. Nisimi’s write-up for Orca Security reports hundreds of confirmed cases from a scan of thousands of repositories. Advisories and published vulnerable ranges are often missing for these fixes, so scanners report the current release as clean.
Elsewhere

DCFinder (Xiaoya Zhu et al., Journal of Computer Security) detects dependency confusion in Python projects that use more than one index. It builds the transitive tree from private indexes and PyPI and checks whether the resolver would select a public version. On 28 real projects it reports 88.7% precision and 83.3% recall, against zero detections from the baseline tools.

Vlad Miricioiu, director of the Software Stewardship Lab and one of my FOSDEM devroom co-organisers, talked to RedMonk about binary dependencies, maintainer burnout, funding models and the Bernies. The Stewardship Lab received $5,000 from Syntax and Sentry towards an annual survey of burnout among open source maintainers.

blocks.text: I love working with designers, in part because (unlike managers and product managers) they’re culturally different from engineers. However, having more than one designer on a team is asking for trouble, and I have complicated negative thoughts about design systems.
Design is a strange role

Designers demonstrate their value immediately. While working on some feature, I’ll typically put together some placeholder UI that I’m reasonably happy with. I then show it to a designer, who strokes their chin and says “hmm, I have some ideas here”. They then go away and produce a mockup UI that is not just clearly better, but better in ways I could not have imagined. There aren’t any other roles at a tech company where you can see the value at a glance.

Designers are an unusual role in other ways, too. Engineering managers, product managers, and engineers all come from broadly the same stock: technical, detail-oriented planners. We are people of the spreadsheet. In fact, many managers and product managers were once engineers: it’s a natural transition. Not so for designers. I’m sure they exist, but I’ve never met any designers who started out as engineers.

Because of this, designers are culturally distant from engineers. In my experience, this is a big positive. I’ve complained before that product managers who were once engineers tend to be worse, not better. Once you start trying to make your own secret technical assessments instead of finding a way to trust your engineering team, you’re doomed: you won’t be able to do it well enough, and the fact that you’re trying will make it impossible to build the trust you need. Designers don’t have this problem at all1.
One designer at a time

So far I have made designers sound like the elves of Middle-earth: mysterious creatures who glide around tech companies dispensing magic. In fact, they are more like the Slavic household spirits, or Domovoy. If you have one Domovoy in a household, it will protect your home against misfortune. If you ever have more than one, they will fight bitterly: “making all sorts of noises, injuring the cattle, turning the master out of his bed, choking people while asleep, etc”. Likewise, a designer can turn your scrappy product into something really beautiful — but you had better have only one designer, otherwise you’re asking for trouble.

The worst experience I have ever had working with designers was on a product where we had three of them: initially just one, who then rotated off the project and was replaced by two very senior designers. As far as I could tell, the first design was pretty good. Unfortunately, the new designers didn’t feel the same way. The very first thing they did was completely redesign the product, which meant I had to rewrite most of the frontend styles. Then they began disagreeing with each other. I think we went back on each page of the product three or four times: one designer would tell me to change X, then the other would change it back, and so on. In the meantime, I was desperately trying to get the product to work.

I knew what I was supposed to do in theory: get everyone in a room talking to each other and hash out a decision. Maybe this would have worked on a different product where the requirements were more stable, but it didn’t work here. The differences in taste, while imperceptible to me, were just too deep. It seemed like everything Designer A produced was slightly wrong in Designer B’s eyes, and vice versa. In the end we just powered through by implementing2 each new iteration until about a week before the deadline, at which point I called in two layers of management as air cover3 to freeze the design in its current state.

These were really good designers! They were far, far better than me at design, and were very nice people who I’d happily work with again. I just think it’s inherently bad to work with more than one designer at a time. I’ve had this experience over and over on different teams and companies. I can only guess4 as to why, but here are two theories:

The classic three-legged stool of product development is made up of engineering, product management, and design. Design is definitely the shorter leg. Almost every team I’ve worked on has had some kind of embedded product management, but only about half the teams I’ve worked on8 have had some access to design (and even fewer have had an embedded designer on the team). Why is that?

Partly it’s because there are products that don’t require design, or at least not in the visual sense that designers provide. Some of the teams I’ve worked on have owned systems with no real visual component: APIs, billing and reconciliation, markdown or pdf rendering9. I have seen companies put designers on these teams anyway, out of some sense that “design thinking” can improve the structure of an API. This is nonsense. Good API design is very important, but it’s a technical job, not an aesthetic one. Designers on these teams typically just sit around or tunnel-vision on some unimportant piece of UI that the team does own (e.g. some internal admin component that no customer will ever see).
